title: Urine Crystals, Stones and Yeast: Struvite, Cystine, Oxalate and Candida
summary: Learn how urine pH sorts crystals, why coffin-lid struvite signals urease-producing bacteria, how to confirm cystine hexagons, why oxalate crystals can be absent in ethylene glycol poisoning, and how to read yeast in a sediment.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 29 Hit 7 (struvite coffin-lid crystals, urease organisms, staghorn calculi), Hit 8 (cystine, uric acid and calcium oxalate/ethylene glycol) and Hit 16 (yeast with pseudohyphae). Checked against Lee 2022, Gaggar 2024, Torricelli 2020, Diri 2018, Kowalczyk 2021, Abou-Elela 2017, Latus 2012, Poloni 2020 and Delanghe 2014. Qualifications: staghorn stones are infection stones in 49–68%, not always struvite (register flag rv-staghorn-not-always-struvite); oxalate crystals were present on admission in only 1 of 6 ethylene glycol patients (register flag rv-ethylene-glycol-crystals-absent); yeast in sediment may be a contaminant (register flag rv-urine-yeast-contaminant). Gaggar 2024 Table 3 appears to have its appearance column offset (coffin lid listed beside amorphous phosphate), so the coffin-lid shape is taken from Lee 2022. Not taught: “budding” as the feature that separates yeast from RBCs and “bacteria are far smaller” (not in the sources read); stone-type percentages (Number Vault).

objectives: Relate urine pH to uric acid, calcium oxalate, struvite and cystine crystals.
Explain how urease-producing bacteria create struvite stones and name the organisms involved.
Distinguish cystine hexagons from look-alikes and interpret absent crystals in cystinuria and ethylene glycol poisoning.
Interpret yeast and pseudohyphae in a urine sediment, including contamination.

scenes.title: Three sediments, one bench
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three urine sediments on one bench. (1) Urine pH 8.0, coffin-lid crystals, culture growing Proteus mirabilis, a large stone filling the renal pelvis on imaging. (2) A teenager with recurrent stones; colourless hexagonal plates. (3) An obtunded adult with metabolic acidosis and raised anion and osmolal gaps; no crystals seen yet; a few oval yeast cells in the same sediment. Question token: “Which finding proves something, and which only suggests?”

cues.text: Three sediments arrive. Alkaline urine with coffin-lid crystals and Proteus in culture. A teenager with recurrent stones and colourless hexagonal plates.
And an obtunded adult with metabolic acidosis, raised anion and osmolal gaps, no crystals yet, and a few oval yeast cells.
Which finding proves something, and which only suggests it?

scenes.title: pH sorts the crystals
scenes.altText: Schematic pH bar from acid to alkaline with crystal cards. Uric acid: forms in acid urine (pH below about 5.5); pleomorphic, rhombic or plate forms. Calcium oxalate: common, also in normal urine; monohydrate as ovals, dumbbells or narrow hexagons; dihydrate as bipyramids (the “envelope”). Triple phosphate (struvite): neutral and alkaline urine; coffin-lid or fern-like forms. Cystine: colourless hexagonal plates in cystinuria. A warning card: refrigeration precipitates phosphates and urates, so crystals are examined on a separate unrefrigerated aliquot.

cues.text: Crystal formation depends on solute concentration, urine flow and urine pH. Uric acid crystals form in acid urine, below a pH of about five point five.
Calcium oxalate is common and appears in normal urine too. The monohydrate forms ovals, dumbbells or narrow hexagons; the dihydrate forms bipyramids, the classic envelope.
Triple phosphate, which is struvite, appears in neutral and alkaline urine as coffin lids or fern-like forms. Cystine forms colourless hexagonal plates.
One preanalytical catch: refrigeration precipitates phosphates and urates, so crystals are examined on a separate unrefrigerated portion.

props.label: Fridge precipitates phosphates and urates: use an unrefrigerated aliquot

scenes.title: Bugs build struvite; genes build cystine
scenes.altText: Struvite card: urease-producing bacteria split urea into ammonia, which yields ammonium and bicarbonate; urine pH rises, phosphate solubility falls, and magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) and carbonate apatite form. Organisms: all Proteus, Providencia and Morganella morganii strains make urease; some Klebsiella and Staphylococcus strains do; only about 1.4% of Escherichia coli do. Staghorn: a stone filling the renal pelvis and at least one calyx; infection stones in 49–68% of staghorns. Cystine card: cystinuria is a mainly autosomal recessive defect of the proximal-tubule transporter for cystine, ornithine, lysine and arginine; hexagonal crystals are highly specific but can be absent (sensitivity as low as 25% in children); the cyanide-nitroprusside screen turns purple above about 75 mg/L cystine (sensitivity about 75%).

cues.text: Struvite is an infection stone. Bacterial urease splits urea into ammonia, which yields ammonium and bicarbonate. The pH rises, phosphate becomes less soluble, and magnesium ammonium phosphate precipitates.

Every Proteus, Providencia and Morganella strain makes urease; not every Klebsiella or staphylococcus does, and only about one and a half percent of Escherichia coli. Staghorn stones fill the pelvis and at least one calyx; about half to two thirds are infection stones.

Cystine stones are genetic. In cystinuria, a mostly recessive defect of a proximal tubule transporter lets cystine, ornithine, lysine and arginine escape into urine. Above its solubility limit, cystine forms hexagonal crystals.
Hexagons are highly specific, but they can be missing: sensitivity can be as low as twenty-five percent in children. A cyanide nitroprusside screen turns purple when cystine is high.

scenes.title: Oxalate, look-alikes and yeast
scenes.altText: Ethylene glycol card: metabolic acidosis with raised anion and osmolal gaps; oxalate crystalluria is described 24–72 hours after ingestion; in one six-patient series only one patient had oxalate crystals on admission; elongated narrow-hexagon calcium oxalate monohydrate crystals are typical. Look-alike card: cystine hexagons are colourless, non-birefringent and dissolve in hydrochloric acid; hexagonal uric acid is pale yellow, polarises and does not dissolve in hydrochloric acid. Yeast card: oval yeast cells, sometimes with pseudohyphae (more if urine stands); mimic red cells, acanthocytes, lipid droplets and calcium oxalate monohydrate; may be a collection contaminant. Hook answers listed.

cues.text: Ethylene glycol poisoning shows metabolic acidosis with raised anion and osmolal gaps. Oxalate crystalluria is described one to three days after ingestion; in one series only one of six patients had them on admission.

Hexagons need a second look. Cystine is colourless, does not polarise, and dissolves in hydrochloric acid; hexagonal uric acid is pale yellow, polarises, and does not dissolve. Oxalate monohydrate can form narrow hexagons too.

Yeast cells are oval, sometimes with pseudohyphae, which multiply if urine stands. They can mimic red cells, acanthocytes, lipid droplets and oxalate monohydrate, and they may simply be contamination.
Back to the hook. Struvite with Proteus suggests an infection stone; the hexagons need solubility and polarisation; and missing oxalate never excludes ethylene glycol.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “No oxalate crystals rules out ethylene glycol” (✓ crystals often absent early; use acidosis, gaps and history); “No hexagons rules out cystinuria” (✓ crystals can be missing; sensitivity as low as 25% in children); “Yeast in sediment = Candida infection” (✓ could be contamination; interpret with collection and clinical picture).

cues.text: Trap one: no oxalate crystals rules out ethylene glycol. No: crystals are often absent on admission. The acidosis, the gaps and the history lead.
Trap two: no hexagons rules out cystinuria. No: the crystals are specific but can be missing, especially in children.
Trap three: yeast in the sediment means Candida infection. No: it can be contamination from a poor collection, so interpret it with the patient.

props.title: ✗ “No oxalate = no ethylene glycol.”
lines: ✓ Often absent early; trust acidosis + gaps

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Alkaline + urease bugs = struvite · acid = uric acid · hexagon = confirm cystine”, “Absent crystals never exclude cystinuria or ethylene glycol · yeast may be contamination”.

cues.text: Read urine crystals with the pH and the patient, because struvite can signal urease-producing bacteria, hexagons need confirmation as cystine, and a missing crystal never excludes cystinuria or ethylene glycol poisoning.

props.label: Alkaline + urease = struvite · acid = uric acid · hexagon = confirm
No crystal ≠ no disease · yeast may be contamination

explanation.what: Plain language: urine carries dissolved salts; when there is too much of one, or the acidity is wrong, it can come out as crystals. Crystals can be an early clue to kidney stones; some are harmless, some point to infection or an inherited disease, and some are artefacts of cold storage. Scientific terms: crystalluria, uric acid, calcium oxalate monohydrate (whewellite) and dihydrate (weddellite), triple phosphate (struvite, magnesium ammonium phosphate), cystine, cystinuria, urease, staghorn calculus, osmolal gap, anion gap, yeast, pseudohyphae.
explanation.why: Crystal formation depends on solute concentration, urine pH and urine flow. Urease turns urea into ammonia, alkalinising urine and precipitating struvite. In cystinuria a proximal-tubule transporter defect lets poorly soluble cystine reach the urine. Ethylene glycol is metabolised to glycolate, giving a metabolic acidosis; oxalate crystalluria is described later, from about 24 hours.
explanation.measure: Examine crystals on fresh, unrefrigerated urine (refrigeration precipitates phosphates and urates). Use pH, shape, colour, birefringence and solubility: cystine is colourless, non-birefringent and soluble in hydrochloric acid; hexagonal uric acid is pale yellow, birefringent and insoluble. Cyanide-nitroprusside screen turns purple above about 75 mg/L cystine. Ethylene glycol: metabolic acidosis with raised anion and osmolal gaps; crystals may be absent early.
explanation.differs: Struvite (alkaline, urease, coffin lid) vs uric acid (acid, below pH about 5.5) vs cystine (hexagonal, genetic) vs calcium oxalate (common, also normal; monohydrate narrow hexagons in ethylene glycol poisoning); yeast vs red cells, acanthocytes, lipid droplets and calcium oxalate monohydrate.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: name the organism behind coffin-lid crystals and a staghorn stone, choose the finding that confirms cystine, recognise that missing crystals do not exclude cystinuria or ethylene glycol, and avoid calling sediment yeast an infection without context.

mnemonic.text: Base builds coffins, acid grows uric, and every hexagon gets a second test.
mnemonic.explanation: Alkaline urine with urease-producing bacteria makes struvite coffin lids; acid urine makes uric acid; hexagons are confirmed (colour, polarisation, solubility) before calling cystine.
mnemonic.limitation: Many crystals occur in normal urine; refrigeration creates phosphate and urate crystals; absent crystals never exclude cystinuria or ethylene glycol poisoning.

analogyLimitations: Crystal and yeast drawings are schematic cards, not micrographs.
Percentages come from single reviews or case series and vary by population.
takeaway: Read urine crystals with the pH and the patient, because struvite can signal urease-producing bacteria, hexagons need confirmation as cystine, and a missing crystal never excludes cystinuria or ethylene glycol poisoning.

questions.stem: A patient with recurrent urinary infections has urine pH 8.0, coffin-lid crystals in the sediment and a large stone filling the renal pelvis. Which organism is most likely involved?

options.rationale: Correct. All Proteus strains produce urease, which alkalinises urine and precipitates struvite.
Incorrect. Although a common urinary pathogen, only about 1.4% of E. coli produce urease, so it is not a major cause of struvite.

options.text: No organism; struvite forms in acid urine
options.rationale: Incorrect. Triple phosphate (struvite) crystals appear in neutral and alkaline urine, and struvite stones form when bacterial urease raises the pH.
Incorrect. Cystinuria gives colourless hexagonal plates, not coffin lids, and is an inherited transporter defect.

questions.stem: Hexagonal plates are seen in a urine sediment. Which finding best supports cystine rather than hexagonal uric acid?

options.text: Colourless, not birefringent, and dissolves in hydrochloric acid
options.rationale: Correct. Cystine is colourless, non-polarising and soluble in HCl; uric acid is pale yellow, polarising and insoluble in HCl.

options.text: Pale yellow and birefringent under polarised light
options.rationale: Incorrect. These features describe uric acid.
Incorrect. Uric acid is the HCl-insoluble crystal; cystine dissolves in HCl.
Incorrect. Heat dissolves amorphous urates; cystine is listed as insoluble on heating.

questions.stem: An obtunded adult has metabolic acidosis with raised anion and osmolal gaps; ethylene glycol ingestion is suspected, but the admission urine shows no oxalate crystals. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Absent crystals do not exclude ethylene glycol poisoning
options.rationale: Correct. Oxalate crystalluria typically appears 24–72 h after ingestion; in one series only 1 of 6 patients had crystals on admission.
Incorrect. Crystals are often absent early, so their absence cannot rule it out.

options.text: Crystals are required before the diagnosis can be considered
options.rationale: Incorrect. Ingestion should be suspected from the history, metabolic acidosis and widened anion and osmolal gaps; ethylene glycol or glycolate levels can be measured.

options.text: The raised osmolal gap excludes a toxic alcohol
options.rationale: Incorrect. A raised osmolal gap is a clue to a toxic alcohol, not evidence against it.

claims.text: pH and crystal type: uric acid in acid urine (< ~5.5); struvite in neutral/alkaline; calcium oxalate common, also normal; shapes.
Refrigeration precipitates phosphates and urates; use unrefrigerated aliquot.
Urease mechanism; urease producers (Proteus, Providencia, Morganella; some Klebsiella, Staphylococcus; 1.4% E. coli); staghorn definition; 49–68% infection stones.
Cystinuria genetics and transporter; hexagonal crystals specific but insensitive; nitroprusside screen; cystine vs uric acid hexagons.
Ethylene glycol: acidosis, raised anion and osmolal gaps; metabolised to glycolate; crystals 24–72 h; 1 of 6 on admission; COM narrow hexagons.
Budding as the feature separating yeast from RBCs; “bacteria are far smaller”; stone-type percentages.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 29 Hit 7 equates struvite with staghorn calculi; Diri 2018 reports staghorn stones are infection stones in 49–68% of cases, and Gaggar 2024 lists triple phosphate crystals in normal subjects too. The lesson teaches “most staghorns are infection stones” (register flag rv-staghorn-not-always-struvite).

Ch. 29 Hit 8 presents calcium oxalate crystals + metabolic acidosis + osmolal gap as the ethylene glycol pattern; Latus 2012 found oxalate crystals on admission in only 1 of 6 patients (crystalluria 24–72 h after ingestion), and calcium oxalate also occurs in normal urine (Gaggar 2024). The lesson teaches that absent crystals do not exclude poisoning (register flag rv-ethylene-glycol-crystals-absent).

Ch. 29 Hit 16 identifies budding ovals with pseudohyphae as Candida; Poloni 2020 notes yeast and pseudohyphae may be sample contaminants and should not be overinterpreted, and pseudohyphae increase when urine stands. “Budding separates yeast from RBCs” was not found in the sources read (register flag rv-urine-yeast-contaminant).
